title: Diljit Dosanjh Is No Longer Indian — and That's the Most Indian Thing About Him
excerpt: The Punjabi superstar's quiet acquisition of US citizenship in 2022 has sparked a national debate about identity, belonging, and what it means to be Indian from abroad.
body:
When Diljit Dosanjh took the stage at Chicago's Allstate Arena on May 10 for the opening night of his AURA World Tour's North American leg, the sold-out crowd — overwhelmingly first- and second-generation Indian-Americans — screamed lyrics in Punjabi with the unselfconscious abandon of people who had found their culture mirrored back at them in a 20,000-seat arena. What most of them didn't know: the man on stage was, legally speaking, one of them.

An investigation by The Indian Express has revealed that Dosanjh acquired United States citizenship in 2022 and has been travelling on an American passport since September of that year. His last Indian passport was issued in 2018. His wife, Sandeep Kaur, is also a US national. He lists a California bungalow as his address on nationality documents. Under Indian law, which does not permit dual citizenship, the implication is stark: Diljit Dosanjh is no longer an Indian citizen.

## 'Kadey v Nahi'

The citizenship report surfaced amid persistent speculation that Dosanjh might enter Punjab politics. Several political figures had publicly courted him, and a think tank had reportedly made a formal approach. Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann went further, claiming the singer was being "pressurised" by the BJP to enter the political arena — a charge that gained urgency after the Lawrence Bishnoi gang claimed responsibility for a shooting outside the Karnal, Haryana home of Dosanjh's manager, Gurpartap Singh Kang.

Dosanjh's response was characteristically blunt: "Kadey v Nahi" — never. He confirmed his US citizenship and said his focus remained squarely on entertainment, music, and his fans. "I have never wanted to be in politics," he posted on social media. "Am Very Happy in My Field."

## An Empire Built Between Two Countries

That field has become extraordinarily lucrative. The AURA World Tour 2026, promoted by Live Nation, spans 13 North American cities including New York's Madison Square Garden and Los Angeles' Crypto.com Arena, with tickets ranging from $78 to nearly $2,000. His previous Dil-Luminati tour had broken multiple records, including a Vancouver show that set a new benchmark for a Punjabi-language concert. He recently appeared on *The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon*, teaching the host Punjabi phrases — a moment that went viral and signalled the mainstreaming of Punjabi culture in American entertainment.

Meanwhile, his Bollywood career continues unabated. He stars in *Border 2*, playing a Param Vir Chakra recipient, and *Main Vaapas Aaunga* — whose title, "I Will Come Back," now reads with unintended irony — releases on June 12 with an A.R. Rahman soundtrack. The film's lead single, "Kya Kamaal Hain," has already topped Apple Music playlists in India.

All of this while entering India on an e-visa.

## A Mirror for the Diaspora

The Diljit citizenship debate has resonated far beyond celebrity gossip because it touches a nerve that 32 million overseas Indians know intimately. India's refusal to allow dual citizenship means that every NRI who naturalises abroad must formally sever their legal bond with the country of their birth. The Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card — a long-term visa, essentially — softens the blow but does not erase it. You can own property, you can visit indefinitely, but you cannot vote, hold public office, or buy agricultural land. You are, in the eyes of the law, a foreigner.

For older generations, this was a private grief quietly processed. For Dosanjh's largely young, globally mobile fanbase, his example raises the question openly: can you be culturally, emotionally, creatively Indian while being legally American? His career suggests the answer is an emphatic yes. He sings in Punjabi, shoots films in Mumbai, wears a turban on Jimmy Fallon's couch, and fills arenas from Vancouver to Orlando with audiences who see no contradiction in any of it.

## What Comes Next

The political subplot may not be finished. CM Mann's claim about BJP pressure, the Bishnoi gang's threat, and the upcoming Punjab elections ensure that Dosanjh's name will remain in political conversation regardless of his wishes. His US citizenship, once a private legal arrangement, is now a fact of public record — and in Indian politics, such facts have long shelf lives.

But on tour in North America this month, none of that seems to matter. The arenas are full. The Punjabi is loud. And the man with the American passport is giving millions of Indians abroad something they rarely get from Bollywood or cricket: the sight of their own hyphenated identity, celebrated at stadium scale.
